title: Discourse on Inequality
author: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
openingChapterLabel: Dedication — To the Republic of Geneva
openingText: Most Honorable, Magnificent and Sovereign Lords: convinced that only a virtuous citizen can offer his country honors it can rightfully accept, I have spent thirty years trying to make myself worthy of paying you some public tribute. Since this fortunate occasion partly makes up for what my efforts could not, I have allowed myself to consult here the zeal that moves me rather than the standing that should authorize me.
about:
The Discourse on the Origin and Basis of Inequality Among Mankind asks a question that sounds simple and turns out to be explosive: where does inequality come from? Rousseau's answer is that natural inequality — differences in strength or intelligence — is trivial compared to the moral and political inequality that civilization creates. He constructs a speculative history of the human race from a solitary, self-sufficient natural state through the invention of property, agriculture, and government, arguing that each step made humans more dependent on each other and more unequal. The famous line — 'The first person who, having enclosed a plot of land, took it into his head to say this is mine, and found people simple enough to believe him, was the true founder of civil society' — captures the argument's force.

Written in 1754 as a response to a prize question from the Academy of Dijon and published in 1755, the Discourse is one of the founding texts of modern political philosophy. It broke with the Enlightenment optimism of Voltaire and the philosophes by arguing that civilization had not improved humanity but corrupted it — that the arts, sciences, and social institutions the Enlightenment celebrated were the very mechanisms of inequality and dependence. The argument influenced the French Revolution, Romantic philosophy, Marx's account of alienation, and every subsequent critique of progress that asks whether modernity has made people freer or more thoroughly controlled.

angleCards.title: The state of nature — thought experiment or history?
angleCards.text: Rousseau describes a solitary, peaceful natural human who needs almost nothing and depends on no one. He insists this is not history but a tool for measuring how far civilization has taken us from our original condition. Watch where he treats it as hypothetical and where he seems to believe it.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Discourse as a thought experiment about human nature — to understand what Rousseau thinks we were before society shaped us, and whether his 'natural man' is a real claim or a philosophical device.

angleCards.title: Property as the origin of all evil.
angleCards.text: Rousseau's most radical claim: the invention of private property is the moment everything goes wrong. Before property, inequality was trivial. After it, every form of domination follows. Track how he builds the case — and whether it convinces.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Rousseau's argument that private property is the root of political inequality — to see exactly how he connects the act of enclosure to slavery, war, and the state.

angleCards.title: Compassion before reason.
angleCards.text: Rousseau argues that natural man has two basic drives: self-preservation and pity — a natural aversion to seeing others suffer. Reason comes later and actually weakens compassion. This reversal of the Enlightenment hierarchy is one of the most provocative claims in the text.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to trace Rousseau's claim that compassion is more fundamental than reason — that pity is natural while reflection is a corruption — and to test it against my own intuitions about what makes people moral.

angleCards.title: Against progress.
angleCards.text: The Enlightenment said civilization improves humanity. Rousseau said it enslaves us. The Discourse is the first systematic argument that progress is not what it seems — that every advance in knowledge, technology, and social organization has come at the cost of freedom and equality.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Discourse as the founding critique of progress — Rousseau's case that civilization has made us more dependent, more unequal, and less free — and to decide how much of it still holds.

cast.name: Rousseau
cast.description: A Genevan philosopher writing from Paris, already notorious for his first Discourse arguing that the arts and sciences had corrupted rather than improved humanity. Here he goes further: inequality itself is not natural but manufactured by civilization. His tone is alternately analytical and prophetic, and the dedication to Geneva — his native city — frames the argument as a personal as well as philosophical act.

cast.name: Natural Man
cast.description: Rousseau's reconstruction of what humans were like before society: solitary, healthy, self-sufficient, moved by self-preservation and pity but not by vanity, comparison, or dependence on others. Natural man is not a noble savage in the romantic sense — he has almost no inner life and no language. He is the baseline against which Rousseau measures everything civilization has added and everything it has destroyed.

cast.name: Amour-Propre
cast.description: The crucial concept Rousseau distinguishes from amour de soi (natural self-love). Amour-propre is the desire to be esteemed by others — to be valued, envied, admired. It arises only in society, when humans begin to compare themselves, and it is the psychological engine of inequality. Once people care what others think of them, they will do anything to be seen as superior. Every social hierarchy follows.

cast.name: Private Property
cast.description: The moment someone enclosed a piece of land and called it his own is, for Rousseau, the founding act of civil society and the origin of every form of political inequality. Property creates the division between rich and poor; the rich then create government to protect what they have; government creates law; and law makes inequality permanent. The entire second half of the Discourse traces this chain.

cast.name: The Academy of Dijon
cast.description: The learned society that posed the prize question Rousseau is answering: 'What is the origin of inequality among men, and is it authorized by natural law?' Rousseau did not win the prize — his answer was too long, too radical, and too hostile to the assumptions behind the question. He published it anyway, and it became one of the most influential texts in the history of political thought.

whyItMatters.title: The Invention of Inequality
whyItMatters.body: The Discourse is the first sustained argument that inequality is not natural but constructed — that the differences in wealth, power, and status that define every known society are not reflections of natural differences between people but products of specific historical developments, above all the invention of private property. This idea is so thoroughly absorbed into modern political thought that it is difficult to see how radical it was in 1755. Before Rousseau, most political philosophy assumed that some form of hierarchy was natural or divinely ordained. After Rousseau, the burden of proof shifted: anyone defending inequality had to explain how it arose and why it was justified. Marx, the socialist tradition, modern egalitarianism, and every critique of structural inequality in the social sciences descend from this text.

whyItMatters.title: The Counter-Enlightenment Begins
whyItMatters.body: Voltaire read the Discourse and wrote to Rousseau that it made him want to walk on all fours. The joke masks the seriousness of the disagreement. The Enlightenment's central commitment was that reason, science, and civilization make life better. Rousseau argued the opposite: that every advance in knowledge and social organization has come at the cost of freedom, equality, and natural compassion. This counter-argument has never gone away. It reappears in Romantic philosophy, in Thoreau's Walden, in the Frankfurt School's critique of instrumental reason, in every contemporary writer who suspects that technology is making us more connected and more lonely at the same time. The Discourse is the original text of that suspicion.

whyItMatters.title: Compassion Before Reason
whyItMatters.body: Rousseau's claim that pity — a natural, pre-rational aversion to the suffering of others — is more fundamental than reason was a direct challenge to the philosophical tradition from Aristotle through Hobbes. If compassion comes before thought, then morality does not need to be reasoned into existence; it needs to be protected from the rationalizations that erode it. This idea influenced Romanticism, shaped the sentimentalist tradition in moral philosophy, and anticipates modern research in moral psychology that finds emotional responses preceding and shaping moral judgments. Whether Rousseau is right about the priority of feeling over reason is still an open question, but the question itself — whether morality is built from the head down or the heart out — is one he forced into the center of the conversation.
